title: Almanac — 52 currencies for the South Bay year
status: Design concepts for a community almanac. Not legal tender, not for sale, no cash value, no redemption, no financial rights.
art: Each note carries one actual numbered Noun, drawn from the official CC0 Nouns trait data using the on-chain seed recorded in public/images/nouns-money/source-100/provenance.json. Fifty-two weeks, fifty-two different Nouns.
rules: Earned by noticing: one note per person who logs that week's sign in the town almanac.
Traded one for one, never sold: a full year is 52 notes.
Wildlife comes first: fences, trails and closed seasons outrank any note.

quarters.name: Rain Quarter
quarters.summary: January to March: winter swell, whales in both directions, the first green and the spring equinox.

quarters.name: Bloom Quarter
quarters.summary: April to June: grunion and terns, May Gray, jacarandas, the blue butterfly and the long day.

quarters.name: Swell Quarter
quarters.summary: July to September: warm water, the Perseids, hurricane swell, shorebirds and the fall equinox.

quarters.name: Wind Quarter
quarters.summary: October to December: Santa Anas, monarchs, first rain, the earliest sunset and the Christmas count.

currencies.name: The Quadrantids
currencies.where: Before dawn, away from street lights
currencies.line: The year opens with a short, sharp meteor shower that peaks around January 3 and 4.
currencies.how: Earned by logging one meteor count before dawn: start time, end time and the meteors you saw. Zero counts too. Trade it one for one with anyone missing week 1.
currencies.source_title: American Meteor Society · meteor shower calendar

currencies.name: Southbound
currencies.line: Gray whales pass the South Bay heading south to the Baja lagoons, most of them in January.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a whale sighting from shore with the time, direction and number of blows. Volunteers count them from Point Vicente every season; the note asks you to watch, not to chase.

currencies.name: King Tide
currencies.where: The high-water line at any beach
currencies.line: Winter new and full moons bring the highest tides of the year, a preview of where the sea is headed.
currencies.how: Earned by photographing the king tide's reach against something that stays put, like a lifeguard tower, a step or a wall, and logging the time. Stay off flooded paths and seawalls.
currencies.source_title: California Coastal Commission · King Tides Project

currencies.name: Winter Swell
currencies.where: The pier and the buoy readout
currencies.line: North Pacific storms send long-period swell down the coast all winter.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the swell from shore next to the nearest buoy's height and period. Watching counts; nobody has to paddle out. Notes trade one for one.

currencies.name: Plover Roost
currencies.where: The fenced roosts on the open sand
currencies.line: Western snowy plovers winter on LA's beaches, roosting in footprints and kelp wrack.
currencies.how: Earned by counting plovers from outside the roost fence with binoculars and logging the count. Dogs on leash, kites elsewhere, and nobody ever steps inside the fence for a note.
currencies.source_title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service · western snowy plover

currencies.name: Grove Lift
currencies.line: Monarch butterflies that wintered in coastal groves warm up, mate and start leaving.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the first monarch you see flying in February, with the time and the temperature. Never shake a branch or touch a cluster to earn one.

currencies.name: Backyard Count
currencies.line: For four days in mid-February, people around the world count the birds where they are.
currencies.how: Earned by counting birds for 15 minutes or more during the Great Backyard Bird Count and sending the list in. One note per person per year, whatever you saw.

currencies.name: Green Week
currencies.line: After winter rain, the brown hills and bluffs turn green almost overnight.
currencies.how: Earned by photographing the same view in October and again in February and logging both. The pair goes into the town almanac as a before and after.

currencies.name: Northbound
currencies.line: The gray whales turn north. Mothers and calves come last, often hugging the shore into May.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a northbound whale or a cow-calf pair from shore. The week 2 and week 9 notes make a set, one for each direction of the same trip.

currencies.name: Spring Forward
currencies.line: Clocks jump an hour ahead and the evening light comes back all at once.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the sunset time the Saturday before and the Sunday after the change. A small note for a small, strange custom.

currencies.name: Poppy Week
currencies.line: California poppies open orange on sunny mornings and close up when it clouds over.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a poppy patch with the time it opened and the time it closed. Look, photograph, leave every flower where it grows.
currencies.source_title: California State Parks · Antelope Valley poppy reserve

currencies.name: Even Day
currencies.line: The spring equinox: day and night run close to even, and the sun sets almost due west.
currencies.how: Earned by photographing the sunset straight down a street that runs east to west and logging the date. The fall note in week 38 makes the pair.

currencies.name: Swallow Return
currencies.line: Cliff swallows return from South America and start rebuilding their mud nests.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the first swallow you see building, with the place and date. Nests stay up; the note is for watching them, not moving them.
currencies.source_title: Cornell Lab · All About Birds · cliff swallow

currencies.name: Grunion Watch
currencies.where: Sandy beaches after a full or new moon
currencies.line: Grunion surf onto the sand to spawn on the nights after full and new moons.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a grunion run from the dry sand: the night, the time and a rough count. Watching only; no fish are taken for a note, and in April and May the season is closed to taking anyway.
currencies.source_title: California Department of Fish and Wildlife · grunion

currencies.name: Sailor Week
currencies.line: In some springs, westerly winds strand thousands of blue by-the-wind sailors on the beach.
currencies.how: Earned by photographing a Velella stranding with a coin or shell for scale and logging the stretch of beach. It may not happen every year, which is what makes the note.

currencies.name: The Lyrids
currencies.line: One of the oldest recorded meteor showers, peaking around April 21 and 22.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a meteor count after midnight on a peak night. Same rules as every meteor note in the almanac: start, stop and what you saw.
currencies.source_title: American Meteor Society · meteor shower calendar

currencies.name: Tern Arrival
currencies.line: California least terns arrive from the south to nest on open sand, including a fenced colony on an LA beach.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the first least tern you hear, the high, scratchy call, from outside the colony fence. They are endangered; the fence is the rule and the note follows it.
currencies.source_title: Cornell Lab · All About Birds · least tern

currencies.name: Eta Aquariids
currencies.line: Dust from Halley's Comet: a pre-dawn shower that peaks in early May.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a meteor count in the hour before dawn. A comet that comes by every 76 years leaves a note you can earn every spring.
currencies.source_title: American Meteor Society · meteor shower calendar

currencies.name: May Gray
currencies.line: The marine layer moves in and stays, gray at dawn and sometimes all day.
currencies.how: Earned by logging, at noon for seven days in a row, whether the sun is out. Seven grays earns the note; any sun resets the count.

currencies.name: Jacaranda
currencies.line: Jacaranda trees bloom purple on the old streets, then drop a carpet on the sidewalks.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the first jacaranda in full bloom on your street and the day its blossoms carpet the sidewalk. Two dates, one note.

currencies.name: Blue Glow
currencies.line: When a plankton bloom comes in, the breaking waves at night can light up electric blue.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a bioluminescent night with a photo and the time, taken from the sand. No swim needed; the waves do the work.

currencies.name: South Swell
currencies.line: Storms in the Southern Hemisphere send long, clean swell north to the South Bay for summer.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the first south swell of the year from shore with the buoy period. Swell from the other side of the planet shows up as a few calm, long lines.

currencies.name: Pelican Lines
currencies.line: Lines of brown pelicans skim the wave faces, more of them as summer goes on.
currencies.how: Earned by counting a single pelican line and logging the number and direction. Biggest line of the season goes on the almanac's back page.
currencies.source_title: National Park Service · Channel Islands brown pelican

currencies.name: El Segundo Blue
currencies.line: El Segundo's own butterfly, small and endangered, flies only while seacliff buckwheat blooms.
currencies.how: Earned by joining a public walk or a habitat workday on the El Segundo dunes. The butterfly is federally endangered, so no one searches off trail; the note marks the work, not a sighting.
currencies.source_title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service · El Segundo blue butterfly

currencies.name: Long Day
currencies.line: The summer solstice: the longest day, with the sun setting at its farthest northwest.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the sunset bearing and time on the solstice. The winter note in week 51 makes the other end of the line.

currencies.name: Sand Crabs
currencies.line: Mole crabs dig in by the thousands where the waves wash back, faster than you can follow.
currencies.how: Earned by counting the crabs in one handful of wet sand, logging the number and putting them all back. Kids are the experts here.
currencies.source_title: Monterey Bay Aquarium · Pacific mole crab

currencies.name: Aphelion
currencies.line: Earth is farthest from the sun in early July, about 3 percent farther than in January.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the noon shadow of a stick at the same spot in early July and in early January. The seasons come from the tilt, and the note says so on the back.

currencies.name: Jelly Summer
currencies.line: Some summers bring blooms of purple-striped and moon jellies close to shore.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a jelly bloom from the pier or the sand with a photo. Look, do not touch, and tell the lifeguards.
currencies.source_title: Aquarium of the Pacific · purple-striped jelly

currencies.name: First Flight
currencies.line: Least tern chicks fledge and start their first clumsy flights over the beach.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a fledgling flight from outside the fence. With week 17 it records the colony's whole season.
currencies.source_title: Cornell Lab · All About Birds · least tern

currencies.name: Delta Aquariids
currencies.line: A slow, faint summer shower that peaks in late July and favors southern skies.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a meteor count facing south on a peak night. A warm-night note.
currencies.source_title: American Meteor Society · meteor shower calendar

currencies.name: Thunderheads
currencies.where: The mountains to the north and east
currencies.line: Monsoon moisture builds towering clouds over the mountains on some July and August afternoons.
currencies.how: Earned by photographing a thunderhead over the mountains and logging the time it peaked. If you hear thunder, go indoors before you log anything.

currencies.name: The Perseids
currencies.line: The year's most popular meteor shower peaks around August 12 and 13.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a meteor count on a peak night. The almanac's biggest night: bring a blanket, bring a neighbor.
currencies.source_title: American Meteor Society · meteor shower calendar

currencies.name: Last Run
currencies.line: The grunion season's last runs, on the nights after the August moons.
currencies.how: Earned by logging an August grunion run. Holding weeks 14 and 33 means you watched the season open and close.
currencies.source_title: California Department of Fish and Wildlife · grunion

currencies.name: Shorebird Return
currencies.line: Sanderlings and other shorebirds come back from Arctic nesting grounds and start chasing waves again.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the first returning sanderling flock you see, with a count. Give them room: a flushed flock loses a meal.
currencies.source_title: Cornell Lab · All About Birds · sanderling

currencies.name: Hurricane Swell
currencies.line: Hurricanes off Mexico can send fast, powerful south swell to the South Bay with little warning.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the swell when a named Eastern Pacific storm is sending waves, with the storm's name. Rip currents run strong; the note is earned from the sand.

currencies.name: Warm Water
currencies.line: Ocean water off Southern California is usually warmest in late summer and early fall.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the water temperature at the same spot once a week through August and September. The warmest reading goes in the almanac.
currencies.source_title: NOAA NCEI · coastal water temperature guide

currencies.name: Cleanup Day
currencies.line: Coastal Cleanup Day: thousands of people pick up the beach on the same morning.
currencies.how: Earned by taking part in Coastal Cleanup Day and logging what your group picked up. One note per volunteer, however much trash you found.
currencies.source_title: California Coastal Commission · Coastal Cleanup Day

currencies.name: Fall Even Day
currencies.line: The fall equinox: day and night even out again, and the sun sets almost due west.
currencies.how: Earned by photographing the sunset down the same east-west street you used in week 12. Same street, same angle, six months apart.

currencies.name: Night Migrants
currencies.line: Songbirds migrate south at night in fall, millions passing over the coast on good nights.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a night's BirdCast forecast and then a morning bird walk. A forecast and a walk earn one note.

currencies.name: Santa Ana
currencies.line: Hot, dry winds blow offshore from the deserts, the air goes clear and fire danger rises.
currencies.how: Earned by logging an offshore-wind day: the humidity, the wind direction and how far you could see. On red flag days the almanac logs, and nobody burns anything.

currencies.name: Monarchs Return
currencies.line: Monarchs arrive back at the coastal groves to cluster for the winter.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the first cluster you see in October, from the path. With week 6 it brackets the monarchs' winter.

currencies.name: The Orionids
currencies.line: More dust from Halley's Comet: the fall shower that peaks around October 21.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a meteor count in the hours before dawn. With week 18 it makes Halley's pair.
currencies.source_title: American Meteor Society · meteor shower calendar

currencies.name: First Northwest
currencies.line: The first real northwest swell of the season wraps in and the winter surf starts.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the season's first northwest swell with the buoy height and period. Week 4 is its winter sequel.

currencies.name: Fall Back
currencies.line: Clocks go back an hour and the evening dark arrives at once.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the sunset time the Saturday before and the Sunday after. With week 10 it closes daylight saving's year.

currencies.name: First Rain
currencies.where: The storm drain at the end of the street
currencies.line: The season's first real rain washes a summer of street runoff into the bay.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the first rain over a quarter inch and staying out of the ocean for the 72 hours after it. The waiting is the work.

currencies.name: The Leonids
currencies.line: A fast meteor shower, famous for rare storms, peaking around November 17.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a meteor count after midnight. Most years are modest, and the note is the same either way.
currencies.source_title: American Meteor Society · meteor shower calendar

currencies.name: Monarch Count
currencies.line: Volunteers count the monarchs wintering in western groves over the weeks around Thanksgiving.
currencies.how: Earned by taking part in the Western Monarch Thanksgiving Count with a registered site volunteer. One note per counter.

currencies.name: Toyon
currencies.line: Toyon, California's holly, turns red with berries just as the birds need them.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a toyon in berry and the first birds you see eating from it. Leave the berries for the birds.

currencies.name: Early Dark
currencies.line: The earliest sunset of the year comes in early December, about two weeks before the solstice.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the sunset time every evening for a week in early December and finding the earliest. The almanac's quiet surprise.
currencies.source_title: timeanddate · Los Angeles sunrise and sunset

currencies.name: The Geminids
currencies.line: The year's richest meteor shower, which starts early in the evening and peaks around December 13 and 14.
currencies.how: Earned by logging a meteor count on a peak night. The coldest meteor note and often the busiest.
currencies.source_title: American Meteor Society · meteor shower calendar

currencies.name: Short Day
currencies.line: The winter solstice: the shortest day, with the sun setting at its farthest southwest.
currencies.how: Earned by logging the sunset bearing and time on the solstice. Hold weeks 25 and 51 and you have the sun's whole swing.

currencies.name: Christmas Count
currencies.line: Audubon's Christmas Bird Count, run every winter since 1900.
currencies.how: Earned by joining a count circle for a day, or counting at a feeder inside one. Birds are dinosaurs, so this note gets one.
currencies.source_title: National Audubon Society · Christmas Bird Count
